pos: n. (the struggle in the Church of Scotland between the evangelical majority and the civil courts, 1833–1843, ending in the Disruption)
etymology: English; the phrase is the title of Robert Buchanan's history of the period (1849).
biblical_def: The Ten Years' Conflict is the name Scotland gave to the decade between the Veto Act of 1834 and the Disruption of 18 May 1843. The question underneath every stage of it was single: whether the courts of the Church of Scotland, or the civil courts of the realm, hold final jurisdiction over the admission of a minister to a parish. The evangelical majority in the General Assembly held that the ordination and induction of a pastor is a spiritual act for which the church answers to Christ alone; the Court of Session held that the church's acts in a legally established and endowed establishment are reviewable at law, and the House of Lords affirmed it. The conflict passed through the Auchterarder, Lethendy, Marnoch, and Stewarton cases, hardened into the Claim of Right of 1842, and ended when 474 ministers left the establishment. 1Co 16:13 is the decade in one line: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conflict as a striving to oppose or overcome, and jurisdiction as the legal power of governing within defined limits.
webster_full: CON'FLICT, n. A striking or dashing together; a fighting; a struggling for victory; contest; strife.
JURISDIC'TION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
ESTAB'LISHMENT, n. The episcopal or other form of religion settled by law; a settled regulation or ordinance.
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Eph 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Ten years of litigation over one question: who admits a minister to a parish.
corruption_paragraphs: The dispute is often described as a quarrel about patronage, and patronage was the occasion rather than the principle. The principle was jurisdictional. If a civil court can compel a presbytery to ordain, then ordination is a civil act performed by churchmen, and the keys have passed out of the church's hands. Eph 6:13 describes the posture the evangelical party took, to withstand “in the evil day, and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13) — and the standing cost them their stipends, manses, and churches.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that jurisdictional questions are not procedural trifles. A church which cannot say who may be its pastors has already lost the power to say what it believes, since the men installed will settle that within a generation. Jud 1:3 commands contending for the faith, and the ten years show what contending looks like in practice: pamphlets, assemblies, court appearances, deposed presbyteries, and at the end a bill of costs paid in full.
roots_summary: Greek gregoreo (G1127), to watch; steko (G4739), to stand fast; agon (G73), a contest.
roots_lines: Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to watch, be vigilant; 1 Corinthians 16:13.
usage: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith” (1Co 16:13) — the decade in one line.
“having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13) — the posture, and its price.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — what it cost to obey.

pos: n. (the act of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, 1834, giving a congregation's male heads of families power to reject a patron's presentee)
etymology: Latin veto, I forbid; act, from Latin actum, a thing done.
biblical_def: The Veto Act was passed by the General Assembly of 1834, the first assembly in which the evangelical party held a majority. It provided that if a majority of the male heads of families in communion with the church in a vacant parish dissented from the patron's presentee, the presbytery should reject him, and no reasons need be given. Its purpose was to restore the congregation's consent to the settlement of its own minister, which patronage had removed; its authors, Chalmers among them, believed the act fell wholly within the church's own spiritual jurisdiction and left the patron's civil right of nomination untouched. The civil courts held otherwise, and every great case of the following decade arose from its operation. Heb 13:17 assumes a people who know and own their pastor, obeying those “that have the rule over you” (Heb 13:17) — which presupposes a relation consented to, not imposed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a veto as a forbidding, the power of rejecting, and a presentee as a clergyman presented to a benefice.
webster_full: VE'TO, n. A forbidding; prohibition; or the right of forbidding; the power of rejecting a proposed law.
PRESENTEE', n. One presented to a benefice; one who is nominated by a patron to an ecclesiastical living.
PAT'RONAGE, n. The right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice; advowson.
scriptures: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
corruption_summary: An act restoring a congregation's consent to the man set over it, and every lawsuit of the decade came out of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Patronage had placed the nomination of parish ministers in the hands of landowners and the crown, with the result that a parish could receive a man it had never heard and did not want. The Veto Act did not abolish the patron's nomination; it required the congregation's acquiescence before the presbytery would proceed to ordination. The New Testament nowhere describes a flock receiving its shepherd by the gift of a proprietor, and 1Pe 5:3 forbids the whole temper of such an arrangement, elders “being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) rather than lords placed over it.

The corruption the act was aimed at is worth naming plainly: a system in which the spiritual office is treated as an item of property. Tit 1:5 gives ordination to the church's officers and Mat 18:17 gives the congregation a standing in its own government, and patronage had set both aside in favour of heritable right. The Veto Act's defect was legal rather than theological — the courts found that an established church endowed by statute could not alter the conditions of settlement unilaterally — and that finding is what forced the church to choose between the endowment and the jurisdiction.
roots_summary: Greek hegeomai (G2233), to lead, rule; tupos (G5179), ensample, pattern; kathistemi (G2525), to ordain.
roots_lines: Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, have the rule; Hebrews 13:17.
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to watch, keep awake; Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “Obey them that have the rule over you” (Heb 13:17) — a relation consented to.
“being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — not lords placed over it.
“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — the church's act, not a patron's.

pos: n. (the lawsuit of 1838–39 in which the civil courts held the Veto Act illegal and ordered the presbytery to take a rejected presentee on trial)
etymology: From Auchterarder in Perthshire, Gaelic uachdar ard, high upland; case, from Latin casus, an occurrence.
biblical_def: The Auchterarder Case was the first and decisive trial of the Veto Act. In 1834 Lord Kinnoull presented Robert Young to the parish of Auchterarder; of about three hundred heads of families, all but two dissented, and the presbytery, acting under the Veto Act, rejected him without taking him on trial. Young and the patron sued in the Court of Session, which in 1838 held by a majority that the presbytery was bound by statute to take the presentee on trial and that the Veto Act was beyond the church's power. The House of Lords affirmed the decision in 1839, Lord Brougham and Lord Cottenham giving opinions that treated the established church's courts as creatures of statute in this matter. The church had now been told by the highest civil authority in the realm what it must do in the ordination of ministers. Act 5:29 is the answer the Assembly gave, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a case as a cause or suit in court, and appeal as the removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
webster_full: CASE, n. A cause or suit in court; as, the case was tried at the last term. In law, a special action on the case.
APPEAL', n. The removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal, as from a common law court to a chancery.
DECREE', n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; a sentence or order of the court.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
corruption_summary: The Court of Session told a presbytery whom it must take on trial, and the House of Lords agreed.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary does not treat the civil judges as villains. Their reasoning had force within its own terms: the Church of Scotland was established and endowed by statute, the patron's right was a civil right, and a church cannot alter by its own act the conditions on which the state has settled its livings. What the judgment could not do was make ordination a civil act. Mat 16:18 settles whose church it is — “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — and a court that orders the laying on of hands has reached past its commission.

Rom 13:1 remains in force and the evangelical party never denied it; they obeyed the civil decree in everything civil, and in 1843 surrendered the endowments the decree governed rather than the jurisdiction it did not. That is the orderly shape of Christian resistance: not defiance of the magistrate in his sphere, but refusal to let his sphere be enlarged. Mat 20:26 describes the only greatness available to a church officer, that “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26), which is not an office a patron can confer.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; exousia (G1849), authority; diakonos (G1249), a servant, minister.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the Assembly's answer.
“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — never denied, only bounded.
“upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — whose act ordination is.

pos: n. (the Banffshire parish settlement of 1841 in which a presbytery obeyed the civil court against the General Assembly and inducted a vetoed presentee)
etymology: From Marnoch in Banffshire, named for St Marnan; case, from Latin casus.
biblical_def: The Marnoch Case was the point at which the Ten Years' Conflict produced an open schism inside a presbytery. John Edwards was presented to the parish of Marnoch in the presbytery of Strathbogie; of the parishioners entitled to object, all but one dissented, and the General Assembly directed the presbytery to reject him. The Court of Session ordered the presbytery to proceed. Seven of its ministers obeyed the civil court; on 21 January 1841 they inducted Edwards while the congregation rose and walked out of the church, leaving the building nearly empty. The Assembly of 1841 deposed the seven from the ministry. The parish of Marnoch left the establishment almost entire at the Disruption two years later. Act 4:19 is the question the seven answered wrongly, whether it be right “in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines induction as the act of putting a clergyman in actual possession of a benefice, and to depose as to divest of office.
webster_full: INDUC'TION, n. The act of introducing; the introduction of a clergyman into the possession and exercise of the office to which he is presented.
DEPOSE', v.t. To lay down; to divest of office; to dethrone; to degrade.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of the pastors of churches within a certain district.
scriptures: Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: Seven ministers obeyed the court and inducted a man his parish had rejected, and the congregation walked out.
corruption_paragraphs: The Marnoch induction is the most vivid scene of the whole conflict because the two authorities had become mutually exclusive: the presbytery could obey the Court of Session or the General Assembly and not both. The seven chose the civil court, and the dictionary names the choice as the error it was. A minister's commission is not held from the magistrate; Mat 20:25 describes dominion exercised by the princes of the Gentiles, and Mat 20:26 says plainly that “it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26).

The second thing the case shows is the congregation. Heb 13:17 commands a people to obey those who have the rule over them and watch for their souls, and the Marnoch parishioners judged, rightly, that a man forced on them by a civil decree over the protest of all but one of them was not such a pastor. Their walking out of the building while the induction proceeded is the Disruption in miniature, two years early and in one parish. 1Pe 5:3 is the standard the seven failed: they acted as men holding an office over a heritage rather than as ensamples to a flock.

usage: “in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God” (Act 4:19) — the seven's question.
“it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26) — the commission is not the magistrate's.
“they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17) — what the parish judged it was not getting.

pos: n. (the suspension and deposition, 1840–41, of seven ministers of the presbytery of Strathbogie for obeying the civil courts against the General Assembly)
etymology: From Strathbogie in Aberdeenshire, Gaelic srath, a valley, with the river Bogie; case, from Latin casus.
biblical_def: The Strathbogie Case is the disciplinary half of the Marnoch affair. When seven of the Strathbogie presbytery's ministers resolved to proceed with the settlement of John Edwards under the order of the Court of Session and against the direction of the General Assembly, the Commission of Assembly suspended them from the exercise of their ministry in 1840, and the Assembly of 1841 deposed them. The civil courts then granted interdicts forbidding other ministers to preach in the parishes of the suspended seven, so that evangelical ministers sent to supply the pulpits preached in fields and barns under threat of imprisonment, and some were fined. The spectacle of a civil interdict against preaching did more than any pamphlet to persuade Scotland that the jurisdictional question was real. Act 5:29 governed the Assembly's act, and Rom 16:17 its ground, to mark those causing division “contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned” (Rom 16:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an interdict as a prohibition, a papal or judicial prohibition, and suspension as a temporary privation of office or powers.
webster_full: IN'TERDICT, n. A prohibition; a prohibiting order or decree; a papal prohibition of the administration of divine service.
SUSPEN'SION, n. A temporary privation of powers, or of the right of exercising an office.
DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of degrading or removing from an office or station; the act of divesting of authority.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
corruption_summary: A civil interdict forbidding ministers to preach, and ministers who preached anyway in the fields.
corruption_paragraphs: The interdicts are the part of this case that persuaded the undecided. A court had now prohibited the preaching of the gospel in named parishes, not on the ground of the preaching's content but to protect the position of the suspended ministers. Men went and preached in the open air. Act 8:4 records the apostolic precedent, that those scattered abroad “went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and there is no record of an apostle asking a magistrate for a licence to do it.

The dictionary holds that the Assembly's discipline was right and that the seven had put themselves outside the church's order. Rom 16:17 directs the marking of those who cause division contrary to received doctrine, and a presbytery that takes its instructions from the Court of Session has made the division. 1Co 16:13 is what the deposed parishes needed and showed: to watch, stand fast, and be strong, in barns, while lawyers argued about which authority could silence a pulpit.

“contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned” (Rom 16:17) — the ground of the discipline.
“went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — what the interdicts could not stop.

pos: n. (the act of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, 1834, giving ministers of chapels of ease full standing in the church courts)
etymology: Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella, a cloak, then a shrine; act, from Latin actum.
biblical_def: The Chapel Act of 1834 dealt with the anomaly of the chapels of ease. Scotland's population had outgrown its parish system, and hundreds of thousands in the cities were served by chapels whose ministers preached, administered the sacraments, and had congregations, but who held no seat in presbytery and whose people had no kirk session of their own. The act erected these chapels into parishes quoad sacra, giving their ministers full standing in the church courts and their congregations proper sessions. It was an act of simple equity and of necessity for the home-mission work Chalmers was pressing. In 1843, in the Stewarton case, the Court of Session held the act beyond the church's power, on the ground that erecting parishes affected civil interests. 1Ti 5:17 is the principle it rested on, that elders who rule well are counted worthy of double honour, “especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapel as a house of worship, a subordinate place of worship, and a parish as the precinct and inhabitants attached to a church.
webster_full: CHAP'EL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship subordinate to a parish church, or annexed to a dwelling.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territory committed to the charge of one parson or vicar, or of other minister having cure of souls therein.
SES'SION, n. In Scotland, the kirk session, the lowest ecclesiastical court, composed of the minister and lay elders of the congregation.
scriptures: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
Let all things be done decently and in order.
To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
corruption_summary: Ministers who preached and baptized but could not sit in presbytery, and a court that said the church could not fix it.
corruption_paragraphs: The anomaly the act removed was indefensible on any New Testament reading. A man who feeds a congregation, administers the ordinances, and watches for souls holds the office described in Eph 4:11 and 1Pe 5:2, and his exclusion from the courts of the church rested on a property distinction between endowed parishes and unendowed chapels. 1Ti 5:17 does not grade elders by the source of their stipend. 1Co 14:40 requires order, and a system in which half the ministers of a city have no vote in its presbytery is disorder dressed as settled law.

The Stewarton decision of 1843 is the second blade of the same scissors that cut at Auchterarder. There the court told the church whom it must ordain; here it told the church it could not organise its own congregations. Taken together the two judgments left the establishment with no jurisdiction that the Court of Session would not review. Heb 12:23 names the church as “the general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23), whose roll is kept in heaven and not in the register of heritable property.
usage: “especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17) — not graded by stipend.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — which the old anomaly was not.
“the general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23) — the roll kept in heaven.

pos: n. (the Claim, Declaration and Protest of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, 1842, asserting the church's spiritual independence)
etymology: Old French claime, a demand; the title echoes the Scottish Claim of Right of 1689.
biblical_def: The Claim of Right — formally the Claim, Declaration and Protest anent the Encroachments of the Court of Session — was adopted by the General Assembly of May 1842 and drafted chiefly by Alexander Dunlop with Candlish and the evangelical leaders. It set out the church's title: that Christ is the only Head of His church, that the government of the church in things spiritual belongs to her own courts, that this had been recognised by statute at the Revolution settlement and in the Treaty of Union, and that the recent decisions of the civil courts were encroachments which the church could not obey without betraying her Head. It claimed the free exercise of that jurisdiction, declared the encroachments unlawful, and protested that if they were persisted in the church would be constrained to surrender the establishment. Parliament did not answer it. Mat 16:18 is the title deed it rested on, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a claim as a demand of a right, and protest as a formal declaration of dissent.
webster_full: CLAIM, n. A demand of a right or supposed right; a calling on another for something due; a challenge of property or ownership.
PROTEST', n. A solemn declaration of opinion, commonly against some act; a formal declaration of dissent.
ENCROACH'MENT, n. The entering gradually on the rights or possessions of another; unlawful intrusion.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: A church set out its title in writing, asked Parliament to respect it, and got no answer.
corruption_paragraphs: The Claim of Right is worth reading as a model of how to state a jurisdictional case. It does not threaten, it does not appeal to sentiment, and it does not deny the magistrate's authority in his own sphere; Rom 13:1 is granted in full. It identifies the one point at issue, produces the statutory and treaty history, and names the consequence of refusal. Act 4:19 and Act 5:29 supply the ground on which the consequence rests: where the two authorities give contrary commands in the same matter, the church obeys God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church should know and be able to state its own constitution before the day it needs it. The Claim was adopted a year before the Disruption, which meant that when 474 ministers walked out they were not acting on a mood but executing a protest already lodged in writing. Mat 16:18 is the whole case in one sentence; everything else in the document is history and statute brought to bear on it.

pos: n. (the withdrawal of 474 ministers from the Church of Scotland on 18 May 1843 to constitute the Free Church of Scotland)
etymology: Latin disruptio, a rending asunder, from dirumpere, to break apart.
biblical_def: The Disruption of 1843 took place on Thursday 18 May in St Andrew's Church, George Street, Edinburgh. The retiring moderator, David Welsh, read a protest instead of constituting the Assembly, laid it on the table, bowed to the royal commissioner, and walked out; Thomas Chalmers followed him, and with them went a procession of ministers and elders down Hanover Street to Tanfield Hall at Canonmills, where they constituted the first General Assembly of the Free Church of Scotland with Chalmers as moderator. Four hundred and seventy-four ministers, about two-fifths of the clergy, left stipends, manses, churches, and schools, and the great majority of the overseas missionaries went with them. Within four years the Free Church had built over seven hundred churches, five hundred schools, and a college. Heb 13:13 describes the act, to go forth “unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disruption as the act of rending asunder, and demission as a lowering, a degrading, the relinquishment of an office.
webster_full: DISRUP'TION, n. The act of rending asunder; the state of being rent asunder or broken in pieces by violence.
SE'CEDE, v.i. To withdraw from fellowship, communion or association; to separate one's self.
STI'PEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
scriptures: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: Four hundred and seventy-four ministers walked out of a church they had won the argument in, and left everything in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Disruption is frequently described as a schism and it was the opposite of one in intent. The outgoing ministers did not claim to be founding a new church; they claimed to be the Church of Scotland, free, and they left the buildings and endowments because those were held on terms they could no longer accept. Heb 13:14 gives the reasoning that makes such a surrender thinkable: “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). Men who believe that can hand back a manse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cost. The ministers who went out had families, no stipend, and in many parishes no building and no legal right to one; some preached for years in tents, quarries, and on the sea-shore between tide marks where no landlord's interdict could reach them. Rev 2:10 is the promise they went out on, “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). The practical lesson is that a jurisdictional principle is only ever proved by what a church will pay for it.

roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
usage: “unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13) — the walk down Hanover Street.
“here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — why a manse can be handed back.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — the promise they went out on.

pos: n. (the instrument signed on 23 May 1843 by which the ministers of the Disruption formally renounced their benefices in the Church of Scotland)
etymology: Old English daed, a thing done; Latin demissio, a sending down, a surrender.
biblical_def: The Deed of Demission is the legal instrument by which the Disruption was made irrevocable. Walking out of an assembly is a protest; the deed, signed at Tanfield on 23 May 1843 and subscribed by the ministers who had left, formally renounced and demitted their status as ministers of the establishment, with the stipends, manses, glebes, and all emoluments attached. It was drawn so that no man could afterwards be said to have kept a foot in both camps or to have left under reservation. Four hundred and seventy-four names went on it. The surrender was reckoned at the time to be worth more than one hundred thousand pounds a year of settled income, given up by men with no fund yet in existence to replace it. Heb 11:38 is what the church said of such men before, that of them “the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deed as a writing containing a contract sealed and delivered, and demission as the relinquishment of an office.
webster_full: DEED, n. A writing containing some contract or agreement, and the evidence of its execution; particularly, an instrument on paper or parchment, conveying real estate.
DEMIS'SION, n. Degradation; a lowering; the relinquishment or surrender of an office or dignity.
BEN'EFICE, n. In the Romish church, all church preferments are called benefices; in England, all church livings below the rank of bishoprics.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: A signed instrument surrendering every stipend and manse, drawn so nobody could claim to have kept one.
corruption_paragraphs: The deed matters precisely because it is a legal document and not a sermon. Protests can be interpreted; a subscribed demission of benefice cannot. Its drafters understood that a half-measure would have left the church's claim ambiguous and its ministers exposed to the charge of wanting the principle and the parsonage at once. Mat 5:10 pronounces blessing on the persecuted for righteousness' sake, and the demission is what turned a vote into a loss.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of making a conviction legally costly on purpose. Heb 13:14 supplies the theology and Mat 25:21 the expectation, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21), said to a steward measured by faithfulness over a few things. The deed is also a useful corrective to the romanticising of 1843: the men who signed it went home to tell their wives that the house was no longer theirs.
roots_summary: Greek axios (G514), worthy; dioko (G1377), to persecute, pursue; pistos (G4103), faithful.
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — said of men who gave up houses.
“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — the deed made it real.
“Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21) — the only wage secured.

pos: n. (the central fund devised by Thomas Chalmers in 1843 by which every congregation of the Free Church of Scotland supported the whole ministry)
etymology: Latin sustentatio, a sustaining, from sustentare, to hold up.
biblical_def: The Sustentation Fund was Thomas Chalmers's answer to the problem the Deed of Demission created: four hundred and seventy-four ministers with no stipends and congregations of very unequal means. His scheme was not a collection but a system. Every congregation, however poor, was to contribute weekly through deacons to one central fund, from which an equal dividend was paid to every minister in the church, so that a Highland parish of crofters and a wealthy Edinburgh congregation drew the same basic stipend, with local supplements permitted above it. The principle he insisted on was that the poorest congregation must give rather than receive, since a church supported by subsidy would never be a church. The fund raised sums that astonished the country and sustained the ministry, the schools, and the college. 1Co 16:2 is its method exactly: “let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” (1Co 16:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sustentation as support, maintenance, and a dividend as a share, the share of interest or profit divided among proprietors.
webster_full: SUSTENTA'TION, n. Support; preservation from falling; use of victuals; maintenance.
DIV'IDEND, n. A share; the share of interest or profit which belongs to each proprietor according to his proportion.
DE'ACON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders; in the Scottish church, an officer charged with the care of the poor and of the church's funds.
scriptures: Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
Gal 6:6
Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.
corruption_summary: Every congregation gives to one fund, every minister draws the same dividend, and the poorest parish gives rather than receives.
corruption_paragraphs: The equal dividend is the part of the scheme that still provokes argument, and Chalmers defended it on two grounds. The first was that an unequal stipend would empty the poor and remote parishes of able men within a generation, since every minister would be bidding for a rich congregation. The second was that the ministry is one office and 1Ti 5:18 attaches the labourer's reward to his labour, not to his parish's rent-roll. Gal 6:6 lays the duty on the taught to communicate to him that teaches, which is a congregational obligation and not a market transaction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Chalmers's insistence that the poorest give. A congregation kept alive entirely by money from elsewhere does not learn 2Co 9:7, that “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7), and never becomes a church in the full sense. 1Co 16:2 supplies the discipline: weekly, by every member, proportioned to what God has prospered him with. The fund worked because it was an application of a text rather than a fundraising campaign.
roots_summary: Greek thesaurizo (G2343), to lay by in store; hilaros (G2431), cheerful; koinoneo (G2841), to communicate, share.
roots_lines: Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up, store; 1 Corinthians 16:2.
usage: “let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” (1Co 16:2) — the method.
“God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7) — why the poorest must give.
“The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18) — the ground of the equal dividend.
